Crane: That's right. Clear as day.
Ms. Adeyemi: Clear as night, surely. It was dark, it was raining, and you were across the street.
Crane: I've got good eyes. Never needed glasses in my life.
Ms. Adeyemi: Good for you. How can you be so sure about the time?
Crane: The church bell. It rang a quarter past just as he came out. You can set your watch by it.
Ms. Adeyemi: Can you? Interesting. And you recognised his face from forty metres, in the rain, at night.
Crane: Not just his face. His coat. Bright yellow. You can't miss it.
Prosecutor Lang: Objection, Your Honour. Counsel is badgering the witness.
Judge Whitmore: I'll allow it, but get to the point, Ms. Adeyemi. We haven't got all day.
Ms. Adeyemi: I'm getting there, Your Honour. Mr. Crane, you said the bell rang at a quarter past. Are you aware the church bell has been out of order since March? The parish fixed it last week.
Crane: Well... maybe I heard a different bell.
Ms. Adeyemi: Maybe. There aren't any others in that part of town, but let's not split hairs. What I find more curious is the coat.
Crane: What about it?
Ms. Adeyemi: The police never released a description of the coat. Not to the press, not to anyone. It's only in the evidence file.
Prosecutor Lang: Your Honour, where is this going?
Ms. Adeyemi: It's going exactly where it needs to. Mr. Crane, the only people who knew about that yellow coat were the police, the killer, and whoever helped the killer get rid of it.
Crane: I... I want to talk to a lawyer.

Judge Whitmore: Order! Order in the court. We'll take a thirty-minute recess. And someone had better get Mr. Crane that lawyer.

In her office, this powerful and frightening man talks about his difficult mother, his unhappy marriage, his teenage children and a strange attachment to a family of ducks that live in his swimming pool. Outside her office, he runs a criminal organisation.

That contrast is the engine of the show. On the one hand, Tony is surprisingly relatable: he worries about his kids, argues about the bills and feels that the good old days are over. On the other hand, he is capable of real brutality. The late James Gandolfini played him with such warmth and menace that viewers found themselves liking a man they knew they shouldn't. This uncomfortable feeling became the model for a whole generation of "difficult men" on television.

The Sopranos was also unusual in its willingness to leave things unresolved. Storylines sometimes simply fade away, dreams go on for whole episodes, and characters rarely learn the lessons we expect them to learn. Some viewers found this frustrating; others felt it was simply more honest than traditional TV. The debate reached a peak with the final episode, which is still argued about today — and which, of course, we won't discuss here.

Is it worth watching now? Definitely, although it requires some patience. The pace is slower than modern streaming hits, and the early-2000s phones and fashions can look dated. But the writing, the acting and the dark humour have aged remarkably well.

title: Subtitles: Your Secret Teacher

Many learners who watch series have the same question: should I turn the subtitles on or off? The honest answer is that subtitles can be a great teacher, but only if you use them in the right way.

First, it helps to know that there are two main types. Native-language subtitles translate the words into your own language, for example Russian. Same-language subtitles show the English words that the actors are actually saying. For learning, the second type is usually much more useful. When you read and hear the same words at the same time, your brain connects the sound of a word with its spelling. Some studies have suggested that this helps learners to understand fast, natural speech better.

Native-language subtitles are not useless, though. If your level is still low, they allow you to enjoy a difficult film without getting lost. However, there is a danger: your eyes simply read the translation, and your ears stop working. You finish the episode, but you haven't really listened to any English.

Here is a simple plan that many teachers recommend. If you are a beginner, start with English subtitles and choose a show you already know well. When you feel more confident, try watching a scene without subtitles first, then watch it again with them to check what you missed. Finally, when you can follow most of the story, turn them off completely and use them only for difficult moments.

One more tip: pause often. If you hear a useful phrase, stop the video, repeat it out loud and write it down. It may feel slow at first, but ten minutes of active watching can teach you more than two hours of passive viewing.

Editors there watch hours of material and choose the moments that will work best. They also decide on the music, which is extremely important. A slow, emotional song or a sudden loud sound can completely change how a scene feels.

Because a trailer is usually prepared months before the film comes out, the editors often work with scenes that are not finished yet. As a result, some shots in a trailer are later removed from the film or changed. If you have ever noticed a scene in a trailer that never appeared in the cinema, now you know why.

There are also different kinds of trailers. A teaser is very short and shows almost nothing, just enough to make fans excited. A full trailer tells more of the story. Some people complain that modern trailers show too much.

Next time you watch a trailer, try to notice how it was built: the music, the rhythm of the cuts and the moment when the title finally appears.

title: Why British and American Series Sound Different
about: British vs American TV series: accents, vocabulary, format
ru: Почему британские и американские сериалы звучат по-разному — и дело не только в акценте

Switch from an American sitcom to a British drama and the difference hits you within seconds. It is not just a question of accent, although that is the most obvious part. British and American series differ in their vocabulary, their sense of humour and even in the way they are written and produced.

Let's start with the sounds. In most American accents, the letter "r" is pronounced after a vowel, so words like "car" and "water" have a clear "r" at the end. In the standard southern English accent you often hear on the BBC, that "r" usually disappears. Americans also tend to turn the "t" in the middle of words like "better" or "city" into a soft, quick sound close to a "d". Of course, both countries have dozens of regional accents: a series set in Liverpool or Glasgow can be a real challenge even for native speakers from London, let alone from Texas.

Vocabulary is the next trap. A British character lives in a flat, while an American one lives in an apartment. The British queue, eat biscuits and take the lift; Americans stand in line, eat cookies and take the elevator. Once you notice these pairs, they become a fun game to play while watching.

The differences go deeper than words, though. Traditionally, a British series has been much shorter: a single season, or "series" as the British say, might have only six episodes, often written by one or two people. American network shows, by contrast, have usually been produced in long seasons of twenty or more episodes by large teams of writers working together. This partly explains why British shows can feel more personal and compact, while American ones build large, familiar worlds you can live in for years.

Humour is perhaps the most famous difference. British comedy often enjoys awkwardness, failure and irony, while American comedy tends to be warmer and more optimistic. The Office is a perfect example. The original British version, created by Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant, ran for just two short series and is painfully uncomfortable to watch. The American remake lasted nine seasons and gradually became much kinder to its characters.

Neither style is better. The best approach for a learner is to mix both: your ears will become more flexible, and you will enjoy a much wider world of stories.

In the hills she finds a strange building: a huge, noisy castle that walks on metal legs. It belongs to Howl, a young and very powerful wizard. title: The Forest Fights Back

Princess Mononoke is one of Hayao Miyazaki's most serious films. It came out in 1997 and was a huge hit in Japan. It is much darker than Totoro or Kiki's Delivery Service, so it is better for teenagers and adults than for small children.

The story is set in medieval Japan. A young prince called Ashitaka protects his village from a wild boar god that has turned into a demon. However, the demon leaves a curse on his arm, and the curse is slowly killing him. To find a cure, Ashitaka travels west.

There he finds a conflict. On one side is Iron Town, led by Lady Eboshi. She is cutting down the forest to make iron. On the other side are the ancient gods of the forest: giant wolves, boars and a mysterious Forest Spirit. With the wolves lives San, a girl who was raised by the wolf goddess Moro. San hates humans and fights them.

The most interesting thing about the film is that there are no simple villains. Lady Eboshi destroys nature, but she also gives work and a home to people nobody else wanted to help. The forest gods are beautiful, but they can be angry and violent. Ashitaka doesn't choose a side. He tries to see both sides clearly and to stop the killing.

The English version was written by the famous author Neil Gaiman. If you want to understand why people call Miyazaki a genius, this film is a good place to start.

title: Your Name: Strangers Who Share a Life
about: Your Name / Kimi no Na wa (2016), Makoto Shinkai
ru: Школьники из Токио и маленького городка просыпаются в телах друг друга.
text:
For decades, whenever someone talked about Japanese animated films, one name dominated the conversation: Hayao Miyazaki. Then, in 2016, a film by a different director became a phenomenon. Your Name, known in Japan as Kimi no Na wa, was written and directed by Makoto Shinkai, and it turned out to be one of the most commercially successful Japanese films ever made.

The premise sounds like a light teenage comedy. Mitsuha is a high school girl living in Itomori, a small, sleepy town in the mountains. She is fed up with country life and dreams of being a boy in Tokyo in her next life. Taki is exactly that: a high school boy in Tokyo who juggles school, friends and a part-time job at a restaurant. One morning, for no clear reason, they wake up in each other's bodies.

The first part of the film gets plenty of laughs out of the situation. Each of them has to survive the other's day, and they start leaving notes and messages to keep track of what happened. Little by little, the two strangers start to care about each other, even though they have never met. Meanwhile, a comet is about to pass close to Earth, and the whole country is excited to watch it.

I won't say more, because the film has a clever twist in the middle, and it works best if you know nothing about it. Let's just say the story becomes much bigger and more emotional than a simple body-swap comedy.

Shinkai's style is instantly recognisable. His backgrounds are almost photographic: sunlight through train windows, rain on city streets, glowing evening skies. The soundtrack by the Japanese rock band Radwimps is an important part of the experience too, and the songs are woven into the storytelling rather than just played on top.

Some critics argue that the film is overly sentimental, and it is true that it isn't shy about pulling at your heartstrings. However, that is precisely why it connected with so many viewers. It captures a feeling most people know: the sense that someone important is missing from your life, even if you can't say who. If you are looking for a first anime film that isn't from Studio Ghibli, you could hardly do better.

title: Cowboy Bebop: Jazz in Outer Space
ru: Культовое аниме о космических охотниках за головами, джазе и одиночестве.
text:
Ask a group of Western fans which anime first made them take the medium seriously, and a surprising number will name Cowboy Bebop. The series was made by the studio Sunrise and directed by Shinichirō Watanabe. It first aired in Japan in 1998, and when it arrived on American television a few years later, it quickly earned a reputation as the anime you show to people who claim they don't like anime.

The show is set in 2071. Humanity has spread across the solar system, Earth is a damaged and half-empty planet, and crime is everywhere. To deal with it, the authorities pay bounty hunters, often called cowboys, to catch wanted criminals. The crew of a shabby spaceship called the Bebop are exactly that kind of cowboy, and they are not very good at making money.

The crew is a collection of lovable misfits. Spike Spiegel is relaxed, lazy and brilliant at martial arts, with a past he refuses to talk about. Jet Black, the ship's owner, is a former police officer who cooks, fixes things and tries to keep everyone out of trouble. Later they are joined by Faye Valentine, a gambler with debts and no memory of her early life, a strange teenage computer genius called Ed, and Ein, a dog who seems suspiciously intelligent.

What really sets the show apart is its mood. Each episode is called a session, and the series borrows freely from westerns, noir detective films, kung fu movies and science fiction. The soundtrack, composed by Yoko Kanno and performed by her band the Seatbelts, is a wild mix of jazz, blues and rock that gives the whole thing its unmistakable energy. Many episodes are self-contained stories, while a handful slowly reveal who these characters were before they ended up on the Bebop.

Underneath the cool style, the show is surprisingly melancholy. Almost every character is running away from something, and the series keeps asking whether you can ever truly leave your past behind.

With only 26 episodes, Cowboy Bebop is easy to fit into a busy schedule. Netflix tried a live-action version in 2021, but it was cancelled after one season, and most fans agreed that the original simply cannot be copied.

WALL-E is a Pixar film from 2008, directed by Andrew Stanton, who had earlier made Finding Nemo. It won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, and many critics consider it one of the bravest films Pixar has ever made.

The story takes place hundreds of years in the future. Humans have left Earth because it is covered in rubbish, and the planet is empty and silent. Only one small robot is still working. His name is WALL-E, and his job is to collect rubbish and press it into neat cubes. He has been doing this alone for about seven hundred years. His only friend is a cockroach.

WALL-E is lonely, but he is also curious. He collects interesting objects he finds, such as lighters and old toys, and he loves watching an old musical on video. His quiet life changes when a spaceship lands and leaves behind a sleek white robot called EVE. She has been sent to look for something important, and WALL-E falls in love with her immediately.

What is most surprising about the film is that the first part has almost no dialogue. The robots communicate with sounds, movements and their eyes, and yet you always understand what they feel. The sound designer Ben Burtt, who had created many famous sounds for Star Wars, made WALL-E's voice.

Later, the film shows where the humans have gone, and it has some sharp things to say about consumerism and caring for our planet. However, it never feels like a lecture, because at its heart WALL-E is a simple love story.

title: Superheroes With Normal Problems

The Incredibles is a Pixar film from 2004, written and directed by Brad Bird. It won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, and even today many people say it is a better superhero film than most live-action ones.

His wife Helen, the former Elastigirl, is busy raising their three children. Violet is a shy teenager who can become invisible, Dash is a hyperactive boy who can run incredibly fast, and baby Jack-Jack doesn't seem to have any powers at all.

When Bob receives a secret message offering him a hero mission, he can't say no. He doesn't tell his family, which, of course, leads to big problems.

The film works because it is really about a family. The superpowers are fun, but the most memorable scenes are about ordinary things: arguments at dinner, a midlife crisis, a teenager who wants to be invisible in every sense. There is also Edna Mode, a tiny fashion designer for superheroes, who steals every scene she is in.

A sequel, Incredibles 2, arrived in 2018, fourteen years after the original.

title: The Monsters in Your Closet

text:
Monsters, Inc. is a Pixar film from 2001, directed by Pete Docter, who later made Up, Inside Out and Soul. It is built on a simple but brilliant idea: the monsters that children are afraid of are real, and scaring kids is just their job.

The monsters live in a city called Monstropolis. Their city gets its energy from the screams of human children, and the biggest company, Monsters, Inc., collects those screams. Monsters go through closet doors into children's bedrooms at night, scare the kids and come back with the energy. However, there is a problem: children today are harder to scare, so there is an energy crisis.

The best scarer in the company is James P. Sullivan, or Sulley, a huge, furry, blue monster. His best friend and assistant is Mike Wazowski, a small green monster with one big eye and a very big mouth. Sulley is voiced by John Goodman and Mike by Billy Crystal, and their friendship is the heart of the film.

Ironically, the monsters believe that human children are toxic and extremely dangerous. So when a little girl accidentally follows Sulley through a door into Monstropolis, it is a disaster. Sulley and Mike have to hide her, and Sulley starts calling her Boo. Soon they discover that something strange is happening inside their own company.

The film is funny, fast and very warm. It also has one of the most exciting chase scenes in animation, through a giant storage room full of doors. In 2013 Pixar released a prequel, Monsters University, which shows how Mike and Sulley first met at college.

title: Soul: What Are We Actually Here For?
ru: Джазовый пианист оказывается в мире душ и вынужден задуматься о смысле жизни.
text:
Pixar has never been afraid of big ideas. It has made films about the emotions inside a girl's head and about what happens to us after we die. Even so, Soul, released in 2020 and directed by Pete Docter, might be its most ambitious attempt yet: a family film that asks what gives a life meaning.

Joe Gardner, voiced by Jamie Foxx, is a middle school music teacher in New York. He is a talented jazz pianist, but his career has never really taken off, and the steady teaching job feels like a compromise he never wanted to make. Then, on the very day he finally gets the chance to play with a well-known jazz musician, he has an accident. Before he knows it, his soul is on its way to the Great Beyond.

Joe refuses to accept this. While trying to escape, he ends up in the Great Before, a soft, pastel world where new souls get their personalities before they are born on Earth. There he is paired with 22, a cynical soul voiced by Tina Fey, who has spent thousands of years avoiding life on Earth because she simply doesn't see the point. Joe needs 22's help to get back to his body; 22 couldn't care less about his plans. Their odd partnership drives the rest of the story.

Visually, the film is a tale of two worlds. The Great Before is abstract and dreamy, full of rounded shapes, and its guides are drawn as single flowing lines. New York, by contrast, is rendered in rich, warm detail, from subway cars to barbershops, as if the animators wanted you to fall in love with ordinary city life. The music follows the same split: jazz arranged by Jon Batiste for Earth, and an electronic score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross for the spiritual world. The score won an Oscar, as did the film itself.

Soul was supposed to open in cinemas, but because of the pandemic it went straight to Disney+, which meant many people watched it at home at a time when life felt strangely on hold. That context made its central argument hit even harder. Without giving anything away, the film gently challenges the idea that a life only counts if you achieve your big dream.

Some viewers found it too philosophical for young children, and that is a fair point. For adults, though, it is one of Pixar's most thoughtful films.

title: The Iron Giant: The Flop That Became a Classic
ru: Как провалившийся в прокате мультфильм о мальчике и гигантском роботе стал классикой.
text:
Some films are hits from the first weekend. Others take years to find their audience. The Iron Giant, a traditionally animated film released by Warner Bros. in 1999, belongs firmly in the second group. It was the feature debut of director Brad Bird, who would later go on to make The Incredibles and Ratatouille at Pixar.

The story is loosely based on The Iron Man, a children's book by the English poet Ted Hughes. The film moves the action to a small town in Maine in 1957, at the height of the Cold War. The Soviet Union has just launched Sputnik, and Americans are nervous about what might be coming from the sky. Hogarth Hughes, a curious nine-year-old with a huge imagination, lives there with his mother, who works long shifts at a diner.

One night Hogarth discovers something astonishing in the woods: a giant metal robot, taller than the trees, that seems to have fallen from space. The Giant eats metal, understands almost nothing about Earth and has no memory of where he came from. Instead of being scared, Hogarth decides to befriend him, hide him and teach him about the world. He gets help from Dean, a laid-back beatnik artist who runs a scrapyard, which conveniently has plenty for the Giant to eat.

Of course, a secret that size is hard to keep. A paranoid government agent arrives in town, convinced that the robot is a weapon, and the tension builds from there. I'll stop here to avoid spoilers, but it is worth saying that the ending has made plenty of grown adults cry.

The heart of the film is a surprisingly deep question for a family movie: are we defined by what we were made for, or by what we choose to do? The Giant may have been built for something terrible, but through Hogarth, he learns that he can decide who he wants to be. The Giant's few words were voiced by Vin Diesel, long before he was a global action star.

Sadly, the studio did very little to promote the film, and it performed poorly at the box office. However, critics loved it, and as it was shown on television and released on home video, it gradually built a loyal following. Today, The Iron Giant regularly appears on lists of the greatest animated films ever made, which proves that a weak opening weekend doesn't have the final say.

o: The Iron Man by Ted Hughes
